clue.text: Vlad must cut in — Spooner's call-girl makes proposal to the gullible

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so the pair must have its initial sounds exchanged

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other, splitting it

parts.note: 'must' means 'have to'
to abridge a text is to cut it
to yell is to call, and Sue is a girl; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: The setter must interrupt as a call-girl propositions a naive client.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call-girl' is not a prostitute here but two words, a call and a girl, whose opening sounds Spooner swaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying mocks credulity: a con man offering to sell a famous bridge, such as the Brooklyn Bridge, he does not own.

clue.text: Crippling one motorway, I tell the police, is about oil giant

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the preceding letters surround what follows, as something that is about another encloses it

parts.note: Mobil is a large oil company
taken as written
to sing is slang for informing to the police
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A tipster confesses to the police about a major oil company crippling the motorway network.
explanation.walkthrough: The oil company goes between the motorway and the second I; to sing is underworld slang for informing.
explanation.definitionFit: Immobilising something leaves it unable to move, which is the sense of crippling it.

clue.text: Correspond with a nameless politician

indicators.note: without a name means the letter standing for name is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a Green politician, losing N for name

explanation.surface: Exchanging letters with an anonymous politician.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name, so a nameless Green is GREE.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that correspond match each other, which is what it means for them to agree.

clue.text: Pop Idol segue highly praised

indicators.note: to pop is to burst, so the letters that follow explode and resettle

parts.note: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A smooth transition on the TV talent show Pop Idol earned rave reviews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop Idol' reads as the TV show, but 'Pop' is the signal and 'Idol' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To eulogise is to speak or write in glowing tribute, so eulogised means lavishly commended.

clue.text: Told off sleeping judge?

indicators.note: someone sleeping lies tucked up inside their bed, so one word goes within another

parts.note: where a sleeper lies
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: A judge caught napping on the bench got a dressing-down.
explanation.walkthrough: A sleeping judge is one lying in bed, so the bed wraps round the judge.
explanation.definitionFit: To berate someone is to scold them angrily, which is to tell them off.

clue.text: Sort of ironic about Stimpy's original canine companion

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes round the other letter
a sort of something is a variant version, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: six letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the original of a word is where it starts, so take its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Stimpy, the cartoon cat

explanation.surface: A wry take on the cartoon cat Stimpy and his dog sidekick Ren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine companion' suggests a pet dog, but a canine is also a tooth, and the incisor sits beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Incisors are the front cutting teeth, neighbours to the pointed canine teeth in the mouth.

clue.text: Cheeky angel representation

indicators.note: a representation renders something in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A painting of a mischievous cherub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' reads as impudent; here it means relating to the cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: Genal is the anatomical adjective for the cheek, from Latin gena.

clue.text: Unlikely end to Tory do, eh — Cleverly shouted at Hunt

parts.note: a tall story is an unlikely one

indicators.note: doing something cleverly means working it with ingenuity, so the letters are rearranged
the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of Tory
four letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Tory party ends implausibly with James Cleverly heckling Jeremy Hunt, both Conservative ministers.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleverly and Hunt look like the two politicians; Cleverly is the signal and Hunt is a fox hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Tally-ho is the cry raised by huntsmen on sighting the fox, so to tally-ho is to give that hunting call.

clue.text: Mike's spoken message

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO alphabet; the 's is 'has'
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: Mike leaves a voice message.
explanation.definitionFit: The moral of a story is the lesson or message it is meant to convey.

clue.text: Not much money in bank lately

indicators.note: one word sits inside the other

parts.note: to bank on is to rely on
a cent is a tiny coin

explanation.surface: Hardly anything left in the account these days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests a building; here it is the verb, as in banking on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean in the recent past, not long ago.

clue.text: Perhaps why issue's raised in political show

parts.note: 'why?' is an example of a query, hence 'perhaps'

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting a word up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: to emit is to issue; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A programme where the question of why something is brought up gets aired.
explanation.walkthrough: Question Time is a long-running BBC current-affairs programme in which a panel of politicians takes audience questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Question Time is a televised political panel debate, so it is a political show.

clue.text: Always first to get into bar … which might explain this

definitions.text: Always first to get into bar … which might explain this

indicators.note: the earlier letters are put inside the word that follows

parts.note: 'all but one' means all bar one
e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of get

explanation.surface: A regular who is always first into the pub, which accounts for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, which it is in the surface, but it is the preposition meaning except. The whole clue describes how a drinker gets a paunch.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer gut is a paunch from heavy drinking, which a habit of being first into the pub would explain.

clue.text: See 1
Ultimately confusing toilets without identifying symbols

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: loo is British slang for toilet

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end of the next word, its final letter

parts.note: last letter of confusing

explanation.surface: Toilets that lack clear signs are confusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside; LOO is everyday British for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Logos are emblems or trademarks that identify a company or brand.

clue.text: Having lost tablets, unfortunately, late leaving for jaunt

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters are muddled
having lost something means some letters are taken away

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so two tablets are two Es
eleven letters, from which two Es are removed before rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone without their pills sadly sets off late on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove both Es from LATE LEAVING, then rearrange the nine letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallivant is to roam about in search of pleasure, much as to jaunt is to take short trips for fun.

clue.text: Board and lodging for priest in the Underworld

indicators.note: giving lodging to someone means housing them inside, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and his realm
a rector is a parish priest

explanation.surface: Room and meals provided for a clergyman in Hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board and lodging' reads as one phrase meaning bed and meals, but it splits after 'Board'.
explanation.definitionFit: A company's board is made up of its directors, so the members collectively are the board.

clue.text: Caught taking type of acid — I'm involved bringing about resolution

parts.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: something involved is wrapped up within something else

parts.note: lactic acid builds up in muscles
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone caught on acid says they're mixed up in sorting things out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type of acid' suggests LSD in the surface, but it is the acid that builds up in tired muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: The climax of a story is where its tension is resolved, so climactic describes what brings the resolution.

clue.text: Like daughters, speaks about youth

indicators.note: a word that is about others goes around them

parts.note: to say is to speak
from the French à la, in the style of
D for daughter, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Speaking of young people, as one might of one's daughters.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter; doubling it makes the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Salad days, Shakespeare's phrase, are one's youthful days of inexperience.

clue.text: Listening intently — debt's twice changed hands

indicators.note: hands are left and right, so two letters for one hand are swapped for the other

parts.note: arrears are unpaid debts; the 's is 'has'

explanation.surface: An outstanding loan passed between two owners.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Rs (right) in ARREARS become Ls (left).
explanation.definitionFit: To be all ears is an idiom for paying full attention to what is said.

clue.text: Sister about to confuse worker in leather

indicators.note: a word placed about another goes around it

parts.note: Sr is the abbreviation for Sister
to addle is to muddle the mind

explanation.surface: A nun sets out to bewilder a leatherworker.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddler makes and repairs saddles and other leather goods for horses.

clue.text: Bird nightly entertains returning primate

indicators.note: returning means heading back, so the letters are read from right to left
to entertain is to hold within, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A bird that sings each night plays host to a monkey coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' looks like the definition, but it is the wordplay; the indri is a lemur.
explanation.definitionFit: The indri is the largest living lemur of Madagascar, and lemurs are primates.

clue.text: Fleming returned with Gallico and another author

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the name reads backwards

parts.note: Ian Fleming, creator of James Bond
Paul Gallico, author of The Snow Goose

explanation.surface: Two novelists, Fleming and Gallico, return together with a third writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another author' follows naturally from two surnames, which supply first names instead.
explanation.definitionFit: V. S. Naipaul was a Trinidad-born Nobel prize-winning novelist, so he is another writer.

clue.text: Singer and presenter Richard getting naked

indicators.note: stripping the clothes off means removing the outer letters

parts.note: Richard Madeley, British TV presenter, without his first and last letters

explanation.surface: A singer and TV host undressing together.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Madeley is a long-standing British daytime television presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adele is the British singer-songwriter, known by her first name alone.

clue.text: Boring, rubbish kind of humour

parts.note: a dead party or place is dull
to pan a show is to rubbish it in a review

explanation.surface: A critic dismissing a dull, worthless style of comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' looks like an adjective; it is the verb, to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadpan humour is delivered with a straight, expressionless face.

clue.text: Hidden diamonds in country

indicators.note: one item goes inside the other

parts.note: the South American country
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Gems concealed somewhere in a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdu, borrowed from French for lost, means concealed or lying in wait out of sight.

clue.text: Hello! Are police back probing who sent this?

definitions.text: Hello! Are police back probing who sent this?

indicators.note: a probe goes inside something, so these letters are put within another word

parts.note: hail is an old greeting
an are is a unit of area, abbreviated a

indicators.note: going back means reading from the end, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: the Met, London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Someone receiving poison-pen letters asks if detectives are investigating the sender.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the recipient's question about abusive letters, so it defines as well as builds.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate mail is abusive or threatening correspondence, the sort whose sender police would investigate.

clue.text: Rita's broken bones

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Rita has fractured some bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken bones' reads as one phrase but splits: 'broken' signals, 'bones' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarsi is the plural of tarsus, the group of ankle bones.

clue.text: Farce! Set right Truss's mismanagement — it's likely to be painful

indicators.note: mismanaged things are handled badly and thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written, possessive dropped

explanation.surface: A call to put right the chaos of Liz Truss's brief, disastrous premiership.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss was the UK prime minister for 49 days in 2022; the surface refers to that fiasco.
explanation.definitionFit: A stress fracture is a hairline crack in a bone from repeated strain, which typically hurts.
